statement: As described in a narrative review by the researchers who ran the studies it summarizes (Greenwald et al., 2014, read from the corrected proof), so that every figure here is second-hand, daily buprenorphine under the tongue, compared with placebo, went with fewer of the brain's µ-opioid receptors free to bind a tracer in PET scans, falling as the dose rose, in people dependent on heroin who were not in treatment; responses to heroin and to hydromorphone, another opioid, were reduced but not abolished at the doses studied; and after a daily 16 mg was stopped, the share of free receptors rose over the three days measured. The authors speak of 'availability' (the share of receptors free) rather than 'occupancy', which cannot be measured directly in people; a fall in availability equals a rise in occupancy only if receptor affinity and the body's own opioids stay constant. Scans began 4 hours after the daily dose, the earliest time studied, which the authors say probably misses the largest fall. In 3 men given 2 mg, then 16 mg, then placebo, double blind (Zubieta et al., 2000), availability against placebo ranged across brain regions from 50% to 64% at 2 mg a day and from 5% to 21% at 16 mg, and withdrawal and heroin-craving scores fell as the dose rose. In 5 volunteers given 32, 16, 2 and 0 mg a day for 12 days each (Greenwald et al., 2003), the regional means were 53% to 72% at 2 mg, 9% to 20% at 16 mg and 2% to 12% at 32 mg; urine tests showed that they kept using opioids between inpatient stays, even at 32 mg a day. In 7 volunteers taking buprenorphine with naloxone (2/0.5, 8/2 and 32/8 mg a day, 14 days each) and tested 15 hours after the dose, against a separate group of 8 on placebo (Comer et al., 2005), self-administration of the larger heroin doses offered decreased only modestly at each maintenance dose, when receptor availability, estimated by a model from behaviour rather than imaged, was 21%, 11% and 6%; the authors' re-analysis suggests that nearly all receptors would have to be occupied, beyond what 32 mg a day achieved, to suppress heroin self-administration fully, and in another of their studies 16 mg a day, or 32 mg every other day, did not fully block the reinforcing effect of injected hydromorphone (Greenwald et al., 2002). The review mentions people who try to get past the block with larger amounts of other opioids, but it reports no data on what happens when they do. In 10 volunteers stabilized on 16 mg a day and then switched, double blind, to placebo (Greenwald et al., 2007), scans 4, 28, 52 and 76 hours after the last dose gave availability of 27% to 31%, 54% to 61%, 65% to 75% and 77% to 94%, against the placebo condition of the 2003 study (other people); after the authors adjusted the 4-hour values to the 2003 study, their fitted curves give 13% to 25% at 4 hours, 37% to 46% at 24 hours, 56% to 73% at 48 hours and 75% to 90% at 72 hours (values between scans are read from the curves, and the adjusted 4-hour range does not match the 2003 study's 9% to 20%). In the same study, the subjective effects of injected hydromorphone were significantly smaller at 4 and 28 hours than at 52 and 76 hours, a recovery the authors call modest. The review's abstract states as results that suppressing withdrawal appears to need 50% availability or less, and that blocking the reinforcing and subjective effects of typical doses of other opioids needs less than 20% (less than 10% against higher-than-usual doses); but its body says that there is no agreed definition of a block and that the availability needed for either effect is not known, its summary says that blockade 'has not been reliably observed under BUP dosing conditions studied to date', and the 20% figure comes from preliminary modelling. The volunteers were relatively healthy, mostly men, aged 18 to 50, without depressive, psychotic or anxiety disorders or substance use disorders other than nicotine, and dependent on heroin; the authors call it unclear whether the findings apply to people seeking treatment or dependent on other opioids; fentanyl was not studied; the scans used buprenorphine without naloxone, although the authors cite data that products under the tongue with and without naloxone have similar effects; and the review reports no results on breathing or overdose, so it says nothing about the risk of overdose when other opioids are used on or after buprenorphine. Certainty: very low. Status: replicated by the same team.
plain: Does Suboxone block other opioids, and for how long? Only partly, in the small laboratory studies summarized in one review by the researchers who ran them. In brain scans of people dependent on heroin who were not in treatment, buprenorphine (the main medicine in Suboxone) took up more of the brain's opioid receptors the higher the daily dose: at 16 mg a day, only about 9 to 20 in 100 receptors were still free 4 hours after the dose. Even so, heroin and another opioid, hydromorphone, still had some effect at the highest doses tested, and the volunteers kept using opioids between their hospital stays. The review mentions people who take larger amounts of other opioids to get past the block, but it has no data on what happens when they do. After 10 volunteers stopped 16 mg a day, the share of free receptors rose steadily over the 3 days of scans, from about 13 to 25 in 100 at 4 hours to about 75 to 90 in 100 at 3 days, and an injected opioid was blunted more at 4 and 28 hours than at 52 and 76 hours. The review's summary names receptor levels needed to block other opioids, but its authors say nobody knows them and that a full block was never reliably seen. The studies had 3 to 10 people each, mostly men, all dependent on heroin; fentanyl was not studied, and the review reports nothing on breathing or overdose.
population: People dependent on heroin who were not seeking treatment, studied as inpatients in laboratory studies by the review's authors, as described in one narrative review: 3 men (Zubieta et al., 2000), 5 volunteers (Greenwald et al., 2003), 10 volunteers (Greenwald et al., 2007; 5 heavier and 5 lighter smokers) and 7 volunteers on buprenorphine with naloxone against a separate group of 8 on placebo (Comer et al., 2005); in the scan studies aged 18 to 50, many fewer women than men, relatively healthy, without depressive, psychotic or anxiety disorders or substance use disorders other than nicotine
exposure: Daily sublingual buprenorphine given by the investigators (study conditions: a liquid at 2 and 16 mg a day in Zubieta et al., 2000; buprenorphine-only tablets at 32, 16 and 2 mg a day, 12 days each, in Greenwald et al., 2003; 16 mg a day for at least 14 days, then placebo, in Greenwald et al., 2007; buprenorphine with naloxone at 2/0.5, 8/2 and 32/8 mg a day, 14 days each, in Comer et al., 2005), with test doses of intranasal heroin or injected hydromorphone given by the investigators; and time since the last dose after stopping 16 mg a day
comparator: Placebo in the same people (Zubieta et al., 2000; Greenwald et al., 2003; doses given in a fixed order); the placebo condition of the 2003 study, in other people (Greenwald et al., 2007); a separate group of 8 heroin-detoxified volunteers on placebo (Comer et al., 2005); earlier against later times after the last dose
outcome: Brain µ-opioid receptor availability (the share free to bind the PET tracer [11C]-carfentanil, as a percentage of placebo) 4 hours after the daily dose or 4 to 76 hours after the last dose; receptor availability estimated by a model from heroin self-administration and ratings (Comer et al., 2005); self-administration and subjective effects of heroin or hydromorphone; the availability thresholds for suppressing withdrawal and for blocking other opioids that the authors infer
magnitude: Greenwald et al. (2014), the authors' summaries and re-analyses of their own studies; no intervals or test statistics printed. Availability, % of placebo, 4 hours after the daily dose: Zubieta et al. (2000; n = 3; liquid) 50–64% at 2 mg/day and 5–21% at 16 mg/day across regions; Greenwald et al. (2003; n = 5; tablets; range of means across seven regions) 53–72% at 2 mg, 9–20% at 16 mg, 2–12% at 32 mg; curve-fit estimates for doses not studied 71–85% (1 mg), 36–55% (4 mg), 20–35% (8 mg; 12–33% in the Fig. 1 legend), 13–24% (12 mg), 4–15% (24 mg). Comer et al. (2005; 7 on buprenorphine/naloxone against 8 on placebo; tested 15 hours after the dose; modelled from behaviour, not imaged): 21–31% (2/0.5 mg), 11–22% (8/2 mg), 6–12% (32/8 mg). After stopping 16 mg/day (Greenwald et al., 2007; n = 10): against the 2003 placebo condition 27–31% at 4 h, 54–61% at 28 h, 65–75% at 52 h and 77–94% at 76 h; adjusted curve estimates 13–25% (4 h), 19–30% (8 h), 24–36% (12 h), 29–41% (16 h), 37–46% (24 h), 56–73% (48 h), 75–90% (72 h); subjective effects of hydromorphone 24 mg intramuscularly significantly smaller at 4 and 28 h than at 52 and 76 h (no statistics printed). Variation between people (2003 study): coefficients of variation at 16 and 32 mg/day 24% and 21% for availability, 39% and 54% for plasma levels, 129% and 109% for withdrawal symptoms; a 3.5-fold range of availability at 2 mg/day in most regions. Heavier smokers (20 or more cigarettes a day, n = 5) had significantly lower availability than lighter smokers (15 or fewer, n = 5) in the 2007 study. Thresholds in the abstract and summary, inferences rather than measurements: withdrawal suppression at 50% availability or less (trough plasma level at least 1 ng/mL); blockade of typical doses below 20% (trough at least 3 ng/mL), from preliminary modelling; below 10% against higher-than-usual doses.

evidence.extracted: The authors use receptor availability (non-displaceable binding potential), an indirect measure, instead of 'occupancy', which they call misleading and not measurable directly in people except with extraordinary methods (to obtain receptor concentration and affinity); if receptor affinity and endogenous opioid levels are assumed constant, a fall in availability is proportional to a rise in occupancy. Measures taken 4 hours after the daily dose, the earliest post-dose time studied, probably reflect less than the largest fall in availability; within-day PET time courses are not feasible. There is no gold-standard definition of clinically meaningful blockade, and neither the availability needed for withdrawal suppression or blockade nor how it varies with patients, opioids and routes is known.

risk_of_bias.note: Seen only through a narrative review by the authors of the studies (card sc_greenwald_2014: narrative-review checklist high; no search, the authors' own studies re-analysed by them). The primary studies cannot be appraised from the review; as it describes them, doses were given in a fixed order (2, 16, then 0 mg; 32, 16, 2, 0 mg), the time course after stopping is referenced to other people's placebo scans, the Comer estimates come from a model fitted to behaviour against a separate placebo group, and values between scans are curve fits.

inconsistency.note: The studies point the same way (availability falling with dose and rising after stopping; blockade incomplete at every dose studied); imaging and modelling give different figures, which the authors say should not be compared.

indirectness.note: Second-hand; volunteers dependent on heroin, not in treatment, mostly men, relatively healthy; fentanyl was not studied; receptor availability and laboratory self-administration stand in for what people ask (whether other opioids work, and the risk of using them), and no breathing or overdose outcome is reported.

imprecision.note: 3, 5 and 10 people in the scan studies and 7 against 8 in the modelling study; no intervals or tests are printed for any availability figure.

publication_bias.note: Not assessable; the review selected the authors' own studies.

grade.reasoning: As the review describes them, the primary studies are within-person comparisons with placebo given in a fixed order, a time course without a concurrent control and a comparison with a separate group, so the evidence starts low (METHODS 6.3: within-person laboratory studies start high only when the order was randomized or counterbalanced, and a claim seen only through reviews starts from the design of the primary studies). Down one level each for risk of bias, indirectness and imprecision: very low (the floor is reached at the first downgrade; the others are recorded for their reasons). The claim rests only on a narrative review, so it stays at draft and its statement says the figures are second-hand (METHODS 6.3). Status replicated by the same team: the fall in availability with dose was seen in two scan studies (3 and 5 people) and incomplete blockade in several studies, all by overlapping authors; the time course after stopping rests on one study of 10 people. The abstract's thresholds are reported as the authors' inferences, not as findings. The doses are the studies' conditions; the claim gives no dosing advice and no timing for using other opioids.
